source: Davidson & Sternberg (1984) The role of insight in intellectual giftedness (Gifted Child Quarterly)
finding: Founding statement of the three-process view. Insight is split into selective encoding, selective combination and selective comparison. The paper links these to giftedness and cites an intervention study showing insight can be trained.
numbers: No numbers in the ERIC record (abstract only). Full text paywalled (SAGE returned 403).
limits: Only the abstract was read. Sample sizes and effect sizes of the intervention study were NOT retrieved; do not quote numbers from this entry.
agent_relevance: Gives a three-part checklist (what to attend to, how to join it, what old knowledge to bring) that maps onto problem framing steps, but it is a description of skills, not a tested algorithm.
quote: Component processes of insight (selective encoding, combination, and comparison) are reviewed

source: Wikipedia: Three-process view
finding: Plain definitions. Selective encoding: telling relevant from irrelevant information. Selective comparison: linking new information to prior knowledge and past experience. Selective combination: putting separate parts together into a new whole.
numbers: None given. Page is a short stub that rests on Davidson 1995 and 2003 and Sternberg & Davidson 1984.
limits: Secondary and thin. Use only for definitions.
agent_relevance: Definitions only; the three operations are close to our operators (filter, retrieve analogue, recombine).

source: Wikipedia: Insight (psychology)
finding: Lists dual-process, three-process and four-stage (Hadamard) accounts side by side. The dual-process line says insight uses a logical analytic system and a fast intuitive system, with the intuitive one more influential.
numbers: Cites Lin et al. 2011 (dual), Davidson 1984 (three-process), Hadamard 1945 (four stage). No effect sizes.
limits: Encyclopedia summary; states no single theory dominates.
agent_relevance: Shows the field has no settled theory, so the schema should not hard-code one account of insight.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem. Frontiers in Psychology 7:1424
finding: Three experiments with classic insight problems, non-insight problems and compound remote associates (CRAs). Insight problems got higher Aha ratings than non-insight problems, but the Aha-accuracy link is only moderate, and some non-insight problems were solved with Aha too.
numbers: Exp 1: N=193 students (nine removed for errors). Accuracy: insight .51, non-insight .54, CRA .37 (insight vs non-insight diff .035, p=.81; CRA lower by .14 and .17, BF10>150). Aha rating: insight 45.2, non-insight 35.0, CRA 30.7 (insight minus non-insight = 10.15, BF10>150). Exp 2 Aha: insight 42.5, non-insight 36.3.
limits: Problem-type labels do not map cleanly to experience. Only the Exp 1 and Exp 2 table was read in detail. Students only.
agent_relevance: A problem label (insight vs analytic) is a weak signal of the process used. A scaffold should key on observed impasse or failure signals (G1), not on guessing problem type.
quote: the positive relationship between Aha and accuracy in insight problems is moderate, and by no means very strong

source: Webb et al. (2016), citing Davidson (1995) The suddenness of insight
finding: Davidson (1995) found that 12-13% of problems classed as non-insight still showed the insight pattern on feeling-of-warmth ratings (sudden jump). So the insight/non-insight split is by solution pattern, not purely by problem type.
numbers: 12-13% of non-insight problems showed an insight pattern of FOW ratings (as reported by Webb et al. 2016).
limits: Second-hand: the Davidson chapter itself was behind a paywall and not read.
agent_relevance: Same lesson: processes vary within problem type.

source: Danek, Fraps, von Mueller, Grothe & Oellinger (2014) Aha! experiences with magic tricks. Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Magic tricks trigger Aha experiences. Participants rated five Aha dimensions; happiness (positive emotion) was most important, impasse least. A participant quote about noticing one small detail was coded as matching selective encoding (Davidson 1995).
numbers: N=50 recruited (48 analysed), 34 video clips, up to 3 viewings each. 41% of suggested solutions came with an Aha. Ratings stable at 14-day retest across all five dimensions.
limits: Self-report, magic-trick domain; the selective-encoding link is an interpretation by the authors of one qualitative quote.
agent_relevance: Supports a newly noticed feature (selective encoding) as one real subjective type of insight; weak evidence.
quote: matches the idea of selective encoding (Davidson, 1995)

source: Hedne, Norman & Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks. Frontiers in Psychology 7:1314
finding: People who said a solution came with insight were more accurate and more confident than non-insight solvers, but warmth ratings did not differ. Confidence tracked accuracy better for non-insight than insight solutions, and insight solvers more often kept their wrong answer on a later recognition test.
numbers: N=51 students (aged 19-31). Accuracy scored by two professional magicians, inter-rater alpha=.911. 8 participants dropped for reporting no Aha; one trick dropped because nobody solved it.
limits: Magic tricks; self-labelled insight. Warmth null result is one study.
agent_relevance: Feeling of insight can mark confidently held errors (Aha is not proof). Fits G3/G4: confidence and sudden certainty must not substitute for a check.
quote: for insight trials the participants were more likely to repeat their incorrect solutions on a subsequent recognition test

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and non-insight problem solving. Memory & Cognition
finding: Classic warmth-rating study. For algebra (non-insight) problems warmth climbed steadily toward the answer. For insight problems warmth stayed flat then jumped late, so people could not predict their own nearness to solution.
numbers: Exact N and ratings not retrieved (paywalled). Pattern confirmed second-hand by Danek 2014 text (opened) which says people cannot judge progress on insight problems.
limits: Not opened this session. Hedne 2016 reports no warmth difference for magic tricks, a boundary condition.
agent_relevance: Argues against asking the model to self-rate progress on stuck problems; progress signals must come from code (G2).

source: Dygert & Jarosz (2026) Navigating the garden path: restructuring as a shared process. J. Intelligence 14(7):128
finding: Creative (insight-type) problem solving correlated with garden-path sentence resolution after removing plain-comprehension variance, and predicted it after controlling for working memory and fluid intelligence. No link to analytic problem solving. Read as support for a shared restructuring process distinct from analytic search.
numbers: Exp I N=85 students. Rebus mean .51, anagram .53, garden path .68, control sentences .85. r(Rebus,GP)=.42, r(anagram,GP)=.27, composite creativity vs GP partial r=.33 (p=.002, R2=.11). GP reliability alpha=.62 (low).
limits: Correlational, single lab, low reliability of GP score; Exp II (WM/Gf control) read at abstract level only.
agent_relevance: Separates restructuring from analytic skill: a second pass that merely thinks harder may not be the same as re-reading the problem differently (reframing operator).

source: Macchi, Poli & Caravona (2025) Dissociable effects of verbalization on solving insight and non-insight problems. J. Intelligence 13(3):36
finding: Concurrent think-aloud hurt an insight problem and helped a non-insight problem: a double dissociation. Authors read this as support for unconscious analytic thought (a third view beyond special-process and business-as-usual).
numbers: N=120 (30 per cell, between-subjects). Deer insight problem: 57% silent vs 13% verbalising. Cryptarithmetic non-insight: 30% silent vs 80% verbalising. Cox model: verbalization z=4.4, beta=1.76, HR 5.79 [2.65,12.67]; interaction z=-4.6, beta=-3.17, HR .04 [.01,.16]. No main effect of problem type (p=.33).
limits: One insight item and one non-insight item only; verbal overshadowing of insight has a mixed replication history.
agent_relevance: Forced step-by-step writing may hurt on problems needing representation change and help on search problems. Supports G1: no forced verbal reasoning everywhere; consistent with our word-puzzle result (92% plain vs 75% forced doubt).

source: Pupil dilation and unconscious analytic thought (2026) J. Intelligence 14(9):211
finding: Eye tracking during an incubation period: people who later solved the insight problem kept high, constant pupil dilation during an unrelated arithmetic task; non-solvers and controls showed falling dilation. Read as sustained unconscious effort and as evidence against a pure System 1 (effortless associative) account.
numbers: N=82 analysed (91 recruited; 8 lost signal, 1 medication). Solvers n=11, non-solvers n=29, controls n=42. EyeLink 1000 Plus, 1000 Hz downsampled to 100 Hz. Group x time interaction significant on pupil size.
limits: Only 11 solvers; pupil size is an indirect effort measure; the incubation interpretation is the authors' theory (UAT), contested.
agent_relevance: Suggests incubation is not idle. For a scaffold: parking a problem plus an unrelated task is a legal design, but it is a bet and cannot be checked by code.

source: Zander, Oellinger & Volz (2016) Intuition and insight: two processes that build on each other or fundamentally differ? Frontiers in Psychology 7:1395
finding: Theory review. Intuition is usually treated as gradual and experience-based; insight as discontinuous. A discontinuity model of insight resembles dual-process accounts in judgment (non-conscious restructuring needed to overcome biased intuitive impressions). Proposes semantic coherence triads (convergent vs divergent) to separate them.
numbers: No new data. Notes only early empirical work by Bowers et al. 1990, 1995 and Dorfman et al. 1996 compared intuition and insight.
limits: Proposal paper; Evans & Stanovich 2013 reply to critics of dual-system models is cited as the current defence.
agent_relevance: Warns that mapping insight = System 1 and analysis = System 2 is too crude.

source: Evans & Stanovich (2013) Dual-process theories of higher cognition: advancing the debate. Perspectives on Psychological Science 8:223-241
finding: Defends dual-process theories against criticisms by redefining the split: Type 1 is autonomous (does not need working memory), Type 2 needs working memory and supports hypothetical thinking. Speed, effort and accuracy are correlates, not definitions.
numbers: No numbers. Existence and role as the current defence confirmed via Zander 2016 (opened) and Crossref.
limits: Not opened; summary from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the fast pass is wrong or the slow pass is right. Check output, not mode (G2/G3).

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model. Psychological Review 117:994
finding: Explicit-Implicit Interaction (EII) theory with a CLARION implementation. Five principles: coexisting explicit and implicit knowledge, simultaneous processing, redundant representation, integration of results, iterative bidirectional processing. Simulates human incubation and insight data.
numbers: Abstract only: 5 principles; simulations of human data (per-task fit numbers not read).
limits: Abstract read via Europe PMC record; full paper not opened. Model fit numbers not retrieved.
agent_relevance: Clearest formal dual-process model of insight: two parallel stores, results integrated, iterate. The integrate-and-iterate loop resembles an agent that runs a fast draft and an explicit check and then compares them.
quote: the simultaneous involvement of implicit and explicit processes in most tasks

source: Gilhooly & Fioratou (2009) Executive functions in insight versus non-insight problem solving. Thinking & Reasoning 15:355
finding: Individual-differences test of whether insight and non-insight problems load on different executive functions. Cited in Macchi 2025 (opened) as part of the case that working memory is not what makes insight hard.
numbers: Numbers not retrieved this session.
limits: Not opened. Only the record (Crossref) and a second-hand characterisation were seen.
agent_relevance: Insight difficulty is about changing representation, not load; adding more working space (longer context) is not the fix.

source: Sternberg & Davidson (1995, eds) The Nature of Insight (MIT Press); lily-pad problem
finding: Edited book that sets the three-process view next to Gestalt, nothing-special and other accounts. The lily-pad problem (60 days to cover the lake, which day is half) is the stock selective-encoding example: people fixate on 60 and half.
numbers: Answer is day 59; common wrong answers are 30 and counting from day 1 (as described in Webb 2016, opened).
limits: Book not opened; the problem description is confirmed in Webb 2016 text.
agent_relevance: Useful as a test item for did-the-model-notice-the-relevant-feature (selective encoding).

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT. Frontiers in AI
finding: ChatGPT solved verbal insight problems at about the most probable human score for both a practice set and a transfer set.
numbers: 15 practice + 15 transfer problems. ChatGPT: 7/15 practice, 5/15 transfer (Fisher exact p<.72 between sets). Humans (n=20): solution rates .55 (practice) and .35 (transfer); human between-set difference not significant (Wilcoxon z=1.29, p<.20).
limits: GPT-3-era model; tiny item set; human n=20; contamination of classic items not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Early parity claim. Later work below shows it does not hold on fresh items.

source: Speed (2023) Assessing the nature of large language models: a caution against anthropocentrism. arXiv:2309.07683
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on a psychometric battery. Both failed both analytic problems completely, but did better on 5 insight problems.
numbers: Analytic problems: human solve rates 55% and 61%; models 0 correct. Insight problems (5): GPT-3.5 1.5-3.5 correct across four runs, GPT-4 4.5/5 on one run. Human per-item correct 44-61%; GPT-3.5 25-75%. Item-level correlation human vs GPT-3.5 r=-0.63 (author says do not weigh it, 4 observations).
limits: Seedling project, tiny item set, partial credit given for non-insight path.
agent_relevance: Items hard for people were not the ones hard for the model: model errors are not human-like, so human insight norms do not transfer to LLM difficulty.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI delivers creative output but struggles with thinking processes. arXiv:2503.23327
finding: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o beat humans on some insight tasks (stumpers, rebus, one character-puzzle comparison) but humans beat GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o on a representational-change task. Models mostly chose by reasoning; humans by transformation. Authors say high insight scores may come from probabilistic inference over prior knowledge, not restructuring.
numbers: Exp 3: 60 humans, 60 model runs per task. Chinese character puzzle: human > GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 by .09, but < GPT-4o by .21. Stumper: human > GPT-3.5 by .20, > GPT-4 by .06, < GPT-4o by .06. Rebus: human < GPT-4-turbo by .32 and < GPT-4o by .39. Representational-change task: humans higher than GPT-4-turbo by .46 and GPT-4o by .31 (p<.001). Strategy: GPT-4o 68.88% and GPT-4-turbo 71.26% reasoning; humans 72.41% transformation.
limits: Chinese-language tasks, one lab; strategy labels come from explanations, which may not reflect the real process.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that LLM success on insight items is retrieval-like; a scaffold needs explicit reframe operators and a code check rather than trust in the model's insight.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo). arXiv:2509.14704
finding: 38 frontier LLMs failed most Japanese riddles that need a representational shift. Reasoning models beat non-reasoning ones but stayed far below people. Models often wrote down the correct candidate and then did not endorse it: a verification failure.
numbers: 201 riddles, 120-item human subset. Non-reasoning (n=16) mean 7.60%, reasoning (n=19) 17.59%, humans about 53% (52.9%). Reasoning vs non-reasoning Cohen's d=0.946. Parameter size did not predict accuracy, release date did. GPT-5 the exception. Human scores bimodal; most LLMs scored very low.
limits: Japanese only; thought-log analysis is exploratory and logs may be post-hoc; search-augmented models scored near human.
agent_relevance: Direct support for selection by code, not by model feeling: the right answer was present but not picked. Add an external check to accept or reject candidates (G2, G3).

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo: thought-log analysis of feeling of rightness
finding: In thought logs, models use phrases like feels closest, but these proxy feelings of warmth or rightness are weaker predictors of correctness than in humans. Authors propose a machine Aha and an AI metacognitive psychology research program.
numbers: Qualitative; proposes a 5-step sequence: candidate generation, pre-answer check, final answer, post-answer check. Future target: a harder version where even GPT-5 scores 33%.
limits: Hypothesis-generating; not a controlled test of dual-process predictions.
agent_relevance: Do not let model-written confidence route the schema (G4).

source: Kargupta et al. (2025) Cognitive foundations for reasoning and their manifestation in LLMs. arXiv:2511.16660
finding: Taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements, 192K traces from 18 models, 54 human think-aloud traces. On ill-structured problems models narrow to rigid sequential processing while humans show more abstraction. Test-time scaffolding of successful structures raised performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems.
numbers: 192K traces, 18 models, 54 human traces, meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers: sequential organisation 55%, decomposition 60%, self-awareness only 16%. Representational restructuring is one listed element (Wertheimer 1945).
limits: Taxonomy built by the authors; the 66.7% is a best-case gain on selected problem types.
agent_relevance: Closest published test of scaffold the structure, do not train. Matches our approach and flags metacognitive control as the neglected piece.

source: Yax, Capdeville & Oudeyer (2024) Studying and improving reasoning in humans and machines. Communications Psychology
finding: Applies dual-process style tests (Cognitive Reflection Test, Linda/Bill) to the GPT-3 family. Larger davinci models gave MORE intuitive wrong answers on CRT while doing better on the matching plain maths. Chain-of-thought and examples raised davinci-003 accuracy, but the same prompts helped humans less.
numbers: 10 OpenAI models; human n=100. DV3 minus DV: correct choice +0.11 (odds ratio .24, p<.001), intuitive response +0.31 (odds ratio .21, p<.001). Example condition on Linda: +0.14 (OR .46, p<.001); Bill +0.05 (p=.424).
limits: CRT items probably in training data (authors say so); GPT-3-era models.
agent_relevance: Shows intuitive-wrong-answer behaviour exists in models and that a step-by-step instruction shifts it. Supports a cheap analytic pass as default on trap items.

source: Cross-study: Orru 2023 vs Zhang 2025 vs Mizumoto 2025, parity versus gap
finding: Verbal insight items: parity or better for LLMs. Representational-change task and NazoNazo riddles: clear human advantage. The difference tracks how much an item can be solved by recall or association versus needing a new representation.
numbers: Orru: ChatGPT 7/15 and 5/15 at modal human score. Zhang: rebus GPT-4o +.39 over humans, but representational-change task GPT-4o -.31. NazoNazo: reasoning models 17.59% vs human 52.9%.
limits: Different languages, models, item sets, years; cross-study comparison is informal (my reading, not a meta-analysis).
agent_relevance: Test our agent on fresh, renewable riddle-like items to avoid contamination (the NazoNazo approach).

source: Branchini et al. (2016) Can contraries prompt intuition in insight problem solving? Frontiers in Psychology 7:1962
finding: Training people to turn a problem's spatial features into their contraries was tested on seven visuo-spatial problems. Mixed models over problems and subjects were used.
numbers: Post-training ratings: understanding M=7.4 (SD 1.67), predicted usefulness M=7.33 (SD 1.86). Accuracy results not read.
limits: Only abstract, methods and manipulation-check text read; outcome numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: A trainable reframe operator (use the opposite) has a precedent, close in spirit to Davidson & Sternberg's training idea.

source: Sandkuehler & Bhattacharya (2008) Deconstructing insight: EEG correlates of insightful problem solving. PLoS ONE 3:e1459
finding: EEG study splitting insight into parts: impasse, restructuring and solution. Extra upper-alpha in right temporal regions for trials that failed then succeeded after a hint, and lower alpha in right prefrontal cortex for high-restructuring trials.
numbers: Frequency results only (upper alpha, right temporal; reduced alpha right prefrontal). N and trial counts not extracted.
limits: Insight problems with hints; neural correlates are loosely linked to cognitive processes.
agent_relevance: Supports splitting insight into impasse then restructuring then solve, which is how the schema already works (impasse detector, reframe operator). See the neural-signatures subfield.

source: Zander 2016 framing: special-process vs business-as-usual vs three-process
finding: Special-process view: a unique restructuring process. Business-as-usual view: same processes as ordinary problem solving. The three-process view sits nearer special-process (insight as skills of attention and combination) but allows gradual training.
numbers: Debate summary; no counts. Macchi 2025 adds a third view (unconscious analytic thought).
limits: Terminology is not fully shared across authors; the placement of three-process view is my reading.
agent_relevance: Competing explanations should not be hard-coded; keep reframing triggered by signals.

source: Nasvytis & Fan (2026) Leveraging speech to identify signatures of insight and transfer in problem solving. arXiv:2605.12970
finding: Think-aloud on matchstick arithmetic. Participants given the same kind of non-obvious solution each time improved faster than those given a different kind each time, and more often spontaneously labelled the kind of problem.
numbers: N=189 participants, five matchstick-arithmetic problems, Same vs Different group. Exact effect sizes not read (abstract and first page only).
limits: Only the abstract and first page were read; speech features not detailed.
agent_relevance: Naming the problem pattern may be part of how insight transfers; suggests a label-the-pattern step after a solve (memory), not before.
